transcript.text: Hi Aditi, good to meet you. I'm part of the team hiring for the Marketing role, and today I'd like to hear about your experience in some depth. We have about 15 minutes, and I'll keep time for your questions at the end. There's no rush, so take a moment whenever you need one. What part of your first term at IIMA has been most engaging so far?
transcript.why: This was a warm-up question to help you settle in. It isn't part of the feedback.

transcript.text: Um so honestly I think the most engaging part for me has been the whole marketing courses so like we had this foundation course and there were a lot of case discussions in class and we had to work in groups which was really fun so we were always connecting different frameworks and like coming up with positioning statements for real brands and even like the Mark-It club activities, especially the D2C brand teardown series, I think that was really hands-on because we deep-dived into how these modern brands are building their channels and customer engagement so it was actually quite different from my audit experience and I felt this allowed us to think creatively but also back it up with some structure so that was quite enjoyable for me
Thanks. Walk me through your background, from SRCC and Deloitte to what you have focused on since starting your MBA.
transcript.why: I moved to your background after hearing what has engaged you during your first term.

transcript.text: Ya sure so basically after my class 12th from Mumbai I went to SRCC in Delhi so did my BCom Honours there and actually like I was preparing for CA side by side so after college I cleared CA and joined Deloitte as an article assistant first so that training was for three years and then post qualification I was made assistant manager with the statutory audit team so most of my work there was with FMCG and consumer durable clients and I got to lead small teams and coordinate with client finance teams um mostly handled the year-end audits and there was lots of checking of controls and also some data analysis work like with sales return and promotions so after two and a half years there I felt I wanted to shift to something more business-facing so decided to join IIMA and since joining here I’ve mainly focused on marketing and strategy electives uh also joined the Mark-It club and did some case competitions so just trying to diversify my experience now away from pure accounting to business and marketing side
What were you trying to solve when you ran a D2C brand teardown series with the Marketing Club?
transcript.why: You described your path from SRCC and Deloitte into marketing activities at IIMA, so we can now explore one of those experiences in more detail.

transcript.text: So um the main thing we were trying to solve with the D2C brand teardown series was basically to understand how these new age brands are actually managing their growth and customer relationships so what we saw was most people in campus knew about the big established brands but not so much about how a Mamaearth or a Sleepr or any of these D2C players were getting traction and building loyal customers so as a team we felt there was this gap in knowledge like the strategies they use on Instagram or WhatsApp or say retention campaigns so our aim was to break down their digital playbooks in a way that was relatable for the batch so we tried to cover what really sets them apart from legacy brands and how they experiment with new channels and all um it was more for learning than just analysing numbers, and a lot of feedback was that it made people curious to try and apply these ideas to cases or even summer prep
You described the series as a team effort. Which part of creating one teardown did you personally own?
transcript.why: Your answer described what the team wanted the series to achieve, so I asked about the part you personally handled.

transcript.text: Ya so in the teardown series actually we usually divided the work like research content design but for the Mamaearth session specifically I took the lead on doing the competitor benchmarking part so basically I was responsible for mapping out how Mamaearth’s social media and influencer campaigns were different from others like Wow or Plum so I looked at their posts frequency, type of collaborations, some customer engagement on posts and tried to spot patterns so then I summarised all of that into slides which we discussed as a group and included in the final presentation and I also spoke about those points during the session so that way I owned one chunk but collaborated on the rest
Thanks, Aditi. Tell me about a time you disagreed with your team or took a stance.
transcript.why: Your answer clarified the part of the teardown you personally handled. We moved on because there was limited time to explore what marketing insight came from that work.

transcript.text: Um okay so one incident that comes to mind is from my audit days at Deloitte actually so we were doing fieldwork for a big FMCG client and there was this issue related to scheme payouts like some of the team felt it was okay to sample only a small set of distributor claims since that’s what the client suggested but I thought we should dig deeper because a few numbers looked odd to me so I pushed for expanding our testing and cross-checking all the distributor claims with the actual system records so at first there was a bit of debate in the team since it meant extra effort and some weren’t convinced it was necessary but I insisted and spoke to my manager separately also so finally we did the expanded work and actually we found those 46 crore of errors so it kind of proved the point and after that everyone agreed it was the right call
Let’s shift to a marketing scenario. How would you choose a launch price for a new snack brand aimed at tier-2 Indian towns?
transcript.why: Your example showed what you personally advocated for, how you handled the team’s concerns, and what resulted from expanding the work. I’m moving to a marketing judgment question next.

transcript.text: Um so actually for a new snack brand in tier-2 towns I think we’d first try to really understand what the local buying power is and what competitors are doing so we’d maybe do some ground surveys and check what are typical price points in the market like do most people prefer five or ten rupee packs or larger value packs and then we’d look at input costs and distribution margins just to see what’s feasible for us to sustain but mostly I think we should be slightly below or at par with local players just for early adoption because in tier-2 towns price sensitivity is quite high and after that maybe we can play with small discounts or bundling so that we attract trial customers but ya basically I’d say a lot depends on competitor pricing and willingness to pay so some field research is must before finalising
If pricing slightly below local competitors reduced your margin, what would determine whether you still chose that approach?
transcript.why: Your answer covered local price research and early adoption, but not how you would balance affordability with margin and the brand’s intended position. I asked about that trade-off.

transcript.text: Um so honestly if we are pricing a bit below and that reduces our margin I think we need to see what our main goal is for the launch phase if our priority is really to just get quick market entry and like build a customer base then maybe taking a short-term margin hit is actually fine as long as it helps us get volume and makes people switch to our brand so we should also look at how long we can sustain that low margin maybe check break-even period and whether we can actually increase prices later once we have some loyalty um and also we need to be sure our lower price is not going to hurt perception or make people think quality is low but ya mostly it depends on whether we can make up that loss with scale or by optimising cost somewhere else so basically it’s more of a strategic call depending on bigger objectives
Thanks. You spent 30 months in audit. What’s pulling you toward marketing after starting at IIMA?
transcript.why: Your answer explained when accepting a lower margin could make sense and what you would monitor before doing so. I’m moving to your motivation for transitioning from audit into marketing.

transcript.text: Ya so actually after spending that much time in audit I realised that while it’s great for understanding business processes and numbers, I was really missing the creative side and also wanted to work closer to building something end to end so in audit we always looked at what’s already happened and it’s more about compliance and finding errors but in marketing I think you get a chance to actually influence consumer behaviour and shape how brands grow which I find much more interesting so after coming to IIMA and getting a taste of those marketing case studies and seeing how much scope there is to try new ideas and think beyond numbers that really pulled me towards marketing I feel it’s a space where you can mix data with creativity and make a more direct impact on the business so ya that’s mainly why I want to explore it now
Which specific experience in audit or at IIMA most influenced your decision to explore marketing?
transcript.why: Your answer explained the appeal of combining data and creativity, but it did not yet identify one specific experience that prompted the move. I asked about that experience to understand what shaped your interest.

transcript.text: Um so I think the one experience that made the biggest impact was actually the D2C teardown project with the Mark-It club at IIMA like in audit I did enjoy the problem solving part especially when we built that Excel analytics template for sales return checks, because it saved a lot of effort and was kind of like process innovation but at IIMA when we did the teardown series I actually felt for the first time that we could take a brand’s story, break it down and see how their choices on even small things like influencer marketing or packaging can change their whole growth so that process of digging into how brands build their audience and then presenting those findings creatively to the batch it just felt different and a lot more engaging for me compared to auditing financial statements so if I had to point to one thing it would be that hands-on exposure to marketing thinking through the club activities here
Let's look at another marketing judgment example. Tell me about a different time when you had to decide which marketing insight or approach to recommend.
transcript.why: Your answer connected your move toward marketing to the D2C teardown series and explained what you found engaging about the work.

transcript.text: Um so actually one example is from the Asian Paints CANVAS case competition that our team did recently so we had to come up with a marketing strategy for a new paints product targeting young urban homeowners and there were a lot of different consumer insights we found in the research like some people cared more about eco-friendliness and others just wanted trendy colours so in our team there was a debate on what to focus on, but I felt after looking at some Instagram and YouTube campaigns that the aspirational aspect, like showing transformation stories, really clicked more with this segment so I pushed for recommending a digital campaign that highlights real home makeovers instead of just features or green claims and in the end our approach was mainly around user stories and influencer tie-ups and that received positive feedback from the judges so that was one place I had to decide which insight to back
Thanks, Aditi. That’s everything from my side. What questions do you have for me?
transcript.why: You described a different marketing decision, including the insight you backed, the campaign direction you recommended, and the outcome from the judges.

transcript.text: Um ya so I wanted to ask actually in your team for this marketing role do new joinees usually get a chance to work on campaign strategy or is it more execution-focused in the first year and also like is there a formal mentorship or feedback process for someone transitioning from a non-marketing background like audit um ya that’s mainly what I wanted to know

Those details can vary by team, so I’d rather not guess about the balance between strategy and execution or the formal feedback process. The recruiter or hiring team can explain how this role is structured. Is there anything else you’d like to know?
transcript.why: You asked about the role's early responsibilities and support for someone transitioning from audit. I answered within what I can confirm and left company-specific details for the recruiter or hiring team.

transcript.text: Um no that covers my main doubts actually, thank you for clarifying and ya I don’t have any other questions right now
Thank you for your time, Aditi. That’s the end of the interview, and your feedback is ready.

topics.question: Let’s shift to a marketing scenario. How would you choose a launch price for a new snack brand aimed at tier-2 Indian towns?
answer_plan: Start with consumer willingness to pay and the price-pack formats common in tier-2 towns.
Compare local competitors, input costs, distribution margins, and the brand's intended quality position.
Choose a starting price based on adoption versus sustainable margin, then state what evidence would make you change it.
Suggest checking trial, repeat purchase, margin, and perceived quality after launch.
topics.example_answer: I would begin by studying willingness to pay, common pack sizes, competitor prices, input costs, and distribution margins in the target towns. I would choose a price that encourages trial without making the economics unsustainable, while keeping the brand's quality position clear. If a lower price reduced margin, I would use it only if the expected increase in trial and repeat purchase could compensate over a defined period. I would test the price in a small market and track trial, repeat purchase, margin, and quality perception before scaling.
